newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook-Diesel set to test support.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook-Diesel set to test support.

text.p: Diesel prices in Asia are poised to test this year's support of $25.00 per barrel, largely due to a steady decline in bid levels by a group of buyers amid plentiful supplies, traders said.
The market has been expecting prices to test support for the past month, but a group of traders supported the price by buying more than 18 million barrels since March 3.
In the past two weeks the traders, Hin Leong Trading, its sister company Sanko Oil and Japanese trader Marubeni International Petroleum Corp, have lowered their purchase prices to $25.50 from $26.50.
The market expected the traders to finish their buying spree with a bang on Friday. But instead, they limited their purchases to two cargoes, signalling that they could be back to buy this week.
Traders said buyers were bent on reducing the level of their bids, although some sellers were trying to resist this.

But they noted that supplies were plentiful amid regional refineries returning from annual maintenance and ample uncommitted arbitrage cargoes, so sale outlets are limited and sellers might be forced to lower prices.

Traders said South Korean refiners are also increasingly aggressive in sales to China, by competing directly with refiners and traders in Singapore for southern China imports, when traditionally they have sold into northern China.

Chinese sources said China has bought at least 750,000 tonnes of diesel in 25 cargoes from South Korea in April and would continue to boost imports from its neighbour in future as their prices were more competitive.

Traders said despite the lack of transparency in its recent import pattern, China has been buying large volumes, as seen in the 793,252 tonnes it took in March, taking its tally for the first quarter to 2.06 million tonnes (15 million barrels).
They said the large imports coupled with smuggling activities are causing severe congestions at the southern Chinese port of Xiamen.
About eight 30,000-tonne vessels and one very large crude carrier containing diesel was said to be waiting off international waters to discharge their cargoes, sources said.
Traders said if the congestion persisted, it could dampen China's near term import demand.
Indonesia has been buying quite actively over the past two months to stock up for national and local polls on May 29, and due to the intermitent refinery problems, traders said.

A source with national oil company Pertamina, said Indonesia imported 3.7 million barrels for April and 4.5 million barrels for May. Traders said even though all refineries in Indonesia are now functioning normally, they would be expected to take about 4.0 million barrels in June.
Traders said the soft diesel prices was also exacerbated by India's purchase of only 270,000 tonnes in its latest tender for June arrival, against market expectations of 600,000 tonnes.
They said while diesel values slid, jet fuel maintained its uptrend on buying support by two Singapore traders, even though regional demand has not picked up.
Traders expected gas oil prices to dip under jet fuel soon, reflected by the swaps market where May regrade was bid at minus 20 cents and offered at plus 20 cents.
At the light ends, traders were jittery about the continued opening of the arbitrage window from the West which would add pressure to prices in Singapore.

They said high aromatic naphtha prices were pressured because of poor demand, triggered by low demand for gasoline. They said a rise in naphtha prices over the week before was mostly due to crude prices, rather than real demand.

Traders said slightly lower light distillate stocks in Singapore last week -- down 277,000 barrels -- did not signal an improving market because regional sale outlets were limited, as seen by low bids for gasoline from China.
Total stock levels remained high at 7.3 million barrels, near the five-year high of 7.5 million.
The market now seeks direction from Taiwan's tender to buy 95-octane unleaded reformate for June 11-30 delivery, which closes on Monday.
The sluggish fuel oil market was given some boost by Taiwan's demand for 76,000 tonnes of 0.5-percent sulphur material. Its tender for June closes on May 7.
The slow regional demand would be balanced by a lack of fuel oil flow from the Middle East, with Kuwait keeping its supplies at home due to summer demand.
Rising prices in the MidEast would also limit the number of cargoes coming to Asia, traders said.
